blocks.html:
The owner slides a forty-page plan across the table. “Two days at a resort, a facilitator, the whole leadership team,” he says. “Ask me what we've done with it since March.”

You have about thirty seconds to say something useful. “That looks like a solid plan” is the wrong answer, and “we can help you build a better one” is worse — he already has a plan, and telling him it's bad tells him the two days were wasted.

What he's actually asking is why it stopped working. The useful answer needs three things from this lesson: what an owner is really after, which of the four ways plans fail he's describing, and what a plan needs in it to survive a busy quarter.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to:

  1. Name the three owner objectives, and hear which one is hurting from what a prospect actually says.
  2. Diagnose a stalled plan as one of the four failure patterns — not as “not enough planning”.
  3. Describe what a plan has to contain, and how the practice runs, for it to still be alive in June.

About 20 minutes, including two short videos.

Practice lead is Jesse Kreun (acting Managing Principal). Every engagement starts with some form of fact-finding assessment, not always a full CSP; a CSP usually recommends OASYS, and OASYS can start without one.

The same January, two companies

Both owners do a two-day planning session and come back with goals. Watch where the two companies are by April.

The well-planned companyThe executed company
The plan saysFive goals for the year, a vision statement, and a revenue target.Five goals, a vision — and the three priorities for this quarter, each with one name against it.
A Tuesday in FebruaryThe weekly meeting covers whatever is on fire. Nobody opens the plan.The weekly meeting opens with the numbers and the three priorities. Two are on track, one isn't, and someone owns it.
By AprilTwo goals are quietly renegotiated and one is forgotten. Nobody notices until Q4.One priority slipped, got solved in February, and the next three were chosen at the quarterly session.
What the owner says“We spent two days on that?”“We're not there yet, but we know exactly where we are.”

The two plans are almost identical. The difference is what surrounds them: a short list of priorities, the numbers that show whether they're moving, and a name against each one. That's the execution gap, and it's the thing an owner feels as “we plan and nothing happens”.

The three owner objectives

Every owner Doug interviews wants the same three things. Learn them as questions an owner asks, because that's how you'll hear them:

  1. Are we achieving our purpose and goals? Mission, vision, values, goals — and often a legacy the owner wants to leave. Even established companies are usually not well aligned on these, and that's typical of our best clients.
  2. Am I gaining time freedom? Owners don't want the business taking more and more of them. Strengthen the leadership team enough and the company becomes self-managing — the owner can step up, step back, or step away.
  3. Are we building enterprise value? The number one lever is reducing owner dependence, so objective two feeds objective three, alongside better financial performance. More value means more options: a financial exit, or an operating exit such as becoming CEO emeritus.

When a prospect talks, listen for which of the three they're describing. “I'm in every decision” is objective two. “I don't know what we're building anymore” is objective one. “We'd be worth more if it didn't all sit with me” is both.

Why strategic planning goes wrong

Four patterns, and they need four different responses:

  • No clear direction — the company reacts to whatever comes up instead of tying decisions to long-term goals. Response: build the plan.
  • Misalignment — every department has its own priorities and they pull against each other. Response: one short list of company priorities that the whole team shares.
  • Poor follow-through — the plan becomes shelfware. This is the execution gap. Response: a rhythm — 90-day priorities, the numbers, and a name against each one.
  • Too busy and too close — leaders are buried in firefighting, carry internal biases, and lack a facilitator. Response: someone from outside the business in the room.

Notice that three of the four are not planning problems. That's why “let's plan again, better” so rarely fixes anything.

How the practice works

  • CEO-level: we're hired by the CEO and work with the leadership team — the people who report to the CEO at a strategic level. Not the whole company, and not around the CEO.
  • Horizontal, not vertical: no industry expertise is needed to deliver it. Industry experience can help build trust, but we aren't selling industry consulting here.
  • A recurring cadence: onboarding and initial implementation, then a plan refresh every 90 days, anchored by a two-day annual session. Best run as an annual plan of work, continuing year after year.
  • Top down, with cross-sell both ways: upgrading the operating system often reveals needs in marketing, sales, operations or leadership that other OneAccord services can meet — and those engagements can lead back to OASYS.
  • The goal is self-sufficiency: clients become educated, disciplined and skilled enough to carry the disciplines on with or without us.

blocks.html:
What a strategic plan is

Strategic planning answers three questions: Where are we now? Where do we want to be? What's the best way to get there? An effective plan is built from connected parts:

  • Vision: what the organization wants to become.
  • Mission: what we offer, to whom, and the unique value we bring.
  • Core values: the timeless principles that shape behaviour and culture.
  • SWOT: internal strengths and weaknesses, external opportunities and threats.
  • Long-term objectives: the big measurable goals for the next few years.
  • 90-day priorities (“Rocks”): the few things that must get done this quarter.
  • KPIs: the numbers that show whether we're on track.
  • Action plans: the projects that achieve the goals.
  • Accountability: who owns what, and how we'll know it's done.

The first four describe the company. The last three are what make the plan a working document instead of a bound one — which is why the forty-page plan on the table is not the problem, and the missing quarter is.

blocks.prompt: A CEO tells you: “Our plan is solid. Marketing has its goals, sales has its own, operations has theirs. Everyone's busy. We just never seem to move as one company.” Which pattern is he describing?
options: A comfortable owner with no pain
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Everyone has priorities; the company doesn't have one short list they share. That's misalignment — and the fix is shared priorities and accountability, not another planning session.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: He has direction and he has activity. What he doesn't have is one short list the whole leadership team is pulling on. That's misalignment.

blocks.prompt: An owner says: “I want out of the day-to-day in three years — but I don't want to sell.” Which of the three objectives is he naming?
options: Achieving the business purpose and goals
None — that's a personal preference, not an owner objective
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right — time freedom, which comes from building a self-managing company. Note the overlap: reducing owner dependence also lifts enterprise value, so objective two usually moves objective three.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Getting out of the day-to-day is the second objective, time freedom — and it's built by strengthening the leadership team until the company runs without him in every decision.

blocks.prompt: Two plans are identical except for one addition. Which one most changes whether the plan gets executed?
options: Three 90-day priorities, each with a named owner and a number that shows progress
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Exactly. A short list, a name against each, and a number — that's what turns a plan into a Tuesday conversation.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: It's the 90-day priorities with an owner and a number. Vision and design improve the document; priorities, owners and measures improve the execution.

blocks.promptHtml:
You're meeting the CEO of a 60-person distribution company. She says: "Honestly, we already do strategic planning. We go off-site every January and come back with a plan. I'm not sure what you'd add."

Write how you'd respond.
rubric: Asks or explores what happens to the plan after January (follow-through, alignment, whether it gets executed) instead of dismissing her process
Names the execution gap: an annual plan without a system to carry it out often becomes shelfware
Explains the 90-day cadence: quarterly refreshes with priorities, KPIs and accountability, anchored by the annual retreat
Connects the value to at least one owner objective (purpose and goals, time freedom, or enterprise value)
Stays consultative and suggests a sensible next step without quoting prices
blocks.coachContext: OneAccord's OASYS Strategic Planning practice (older materials and videos call it SPE, Strategic Planning and Execution; Doug sometimes says 'Oasis') helps clients build a strategic plan AND upgrade their Business Operating System (BOS) so the plan actually gets executed. OASYS is OneAccord's branded BOS, built on the Ninety OS model and run on the ninety.io software platform. Doug Hall presents the training videos and helped launch the practice; he has coached business operating systems since 2016 (first EOS-certified implementer in Washington State in 2017, later Pinnacle Business Guides and Scaling Up), and takes an independent, best-of-breed approach. Jesse Kreun is acting Managing Principal and leads the OASYS practice; questions about the practice go to Jesse. A CSP and OASYS are independent offerings: every engagement starts with some form of fact-finding assessment, which is not always a full CSP; a CSP usually recommends OASYS, and OASYS can begin without a CSP. Three owner objectives: (1) achieve the business purpose and goals (mission, vision, values, legacy, aligned team); (2) increase the owner's time freedom by building a self-managing company with a strong leadership team; (3) optimize enterprise value, mainly by reducing owner dependence and improving financial performance, which opens exit options including a financial exit or an operating exit (e.g. CEO emeritus). If an owner is comfortable on all three, they won't buy; there must be pain in at least one, or a vague dissatisfaction, a desire to be a 'category of one', or a sense the owner can't take the company to the next level alone (humility and hunger). Common strategic planning failures: no clear direction, misaligned teams, poor follow-through, 'shelfware' plans that never get executed (the execution gap), firefighting, bias, complexity. Strategic planning answers: where are we now, where do we want to be, how do we get there. Building blocks: vision, mission, core values, SWOT, long-term objectives, 90-day priorities ('Rocks'), KPIs, action plans, accountability structure. The practice is horizontal (no industry expertise needed), hired by the CEO, and works with the leadership team (the CEO's strategic direct reports). Engagement: onboarding and initial implementation, then a strategic plan refresh every 90 days anchored by an annual 2-day off-site retreat, typically as an annual plan of work billed as a monthly retainer. Do not quote prices; a managing principal guides pricing. It is a top-down upgrade that can cross-sell into functional work (marketing, sales, operations, interim/fractional leaders) and vice versa; OneAccord refers out legal and some CFO work. Every company that makes payroll already has a BOS: its current way of leading and managing (often informal, like a fish not knowing it's in water), shaped by the founder, shiny objects the CEO brings back from peer groups, and new managers' habits. Typical informal BOS tools: occasional off-site planning, a maybe-written strategic plan, a budget, monthly financials, weekly staff meetings, one-on-ones, all-hands, annual performance reviews. Upgrading means getting uncomfortable before getting comfortable again, so change management matters. Costs of an informal BOS: chaos, wasted time, inconsistent results, stalled growth, over-reliance on individuals, reduced company value. Deming: every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets. Owners can upgrade functions (marketing, sales, ops, finance) or upgrade the BOS and leadership team; prospects for OASYS usually find the leadership team has become the limiting factor. BOS lineage: Gerber (E-Myth), Jack Stack (Great Game of Business), Andy Grove and John Doerr (OKRs), Verne Harnish (Rockefeller Habits, Scaling Up), Gino Wickman (EOS/Traction), Franklin Covey (4 Disciplines of Execution), plus Lencioni and Collins; Ninety OS is the first software-based BOS and covers the best of EOS, 4DX, OKRs and parts of Scaling Up. Foundational tools: one-page strategic plan (core values, purpose, 10-year, 3-year, 1-year goals, 90-day Rocks), org chart with functional accountability, KPI scorecards with lead and lag measures, weekly team meetings with a set agenda, quarterly planning cadence. Ninety OS has 9 core competencies (vision, customer, goals, people, structure, data, meetings, process, enterprise value), continuously improved by working the system. ninety.io holds vision and planning, scorecard, Rocks, issues, meeting rhythms, people tools, processes, to-dos. Client options: do-it-yourself alone (read Traction), DIY with group coaching, or done-for-you implementer coaching (OneAccord's recommended full engagement). The coach is like a sports coach on the sidelines: not better at the game, better at watching and coaching. OneAccord always recommends the full coached engagement but can help budget-limited clients self-implement on ninety.io and stay their go-to resource. Success = steady improvement on ten factors (solid strategy, shared vision, right people in right seats, teamwork, right numbers/KPIs, consistent execution, solving issues / self-managing team, getting the right stuff done in 90-day focus, financial performance, enterprise value), not a single end goal. Process: baseline benchmarks (OneAccord business assessment, enterprise value appraisal, behavioral assessments such as DISC or Predictive Index, team tools such as Working Genius and Five Dysfunctions trust-building) -> situation analysis and proposal -> agreement with owner/CEO -> implementation workshops (foundations, goals, vision; full days or several half days, virtual or in person) -> coach the weekly team meetings and roll the agenda down -> schedule quarterly planning dates for a rolling 12 months -> facilitate 90-day off-sites (ideally in person) -> the first two-day session IS year one's annual session and carries the Foundation work -> three one-day quarterlies plus one two-day annual every year, ongoing with no planned end -> 'graduate' is allowed if the client can sustain the cadence itself, but it is not the design goal.

blocks.promptHtml:
Different conditions: this company already runs a planning rhythm — and it still isn't working.

The CEO of a $25M services firm tells you: “We do this properly. Two-day off-site every January, quarterly reviews with dates in the calendar, and we always leave with a plan. But ask three of my leaders what this quarter's top priority is and you'll get three different answers.”

What do you say, and what do you want to find out before you recommend anything?
rubric: Recognises that the planning isn't the problem — the cadence exists and works — and names ownership and alignment as the gap
Asks how priorities are set and reviewed between sessions (who chooses them, who owns each one, what number shows progress) instead of proposing a re-plan
Explains what a plan needs to hold people together: a short shared list, one named owner per priority, and a measure for each
Does not dismiss their existing process or imply the last off-site was wasted, which would cost you the room
Suggests a specific, low-pressure next step and does not quote a price or a scope
blocks.coachContext: This company has the rhythm and not the ownership. The four failure patterns are: no clear direction; misalignment; poor follow-through (the execution gap, shelfware); and too busy/too close. This is misalignment plus weak ownership, not a planning gap, so recommending a re-plan is the wrong move. What a strategic plan must contain: vision, mission, core values, SWOT, long-term objectives, 90-day priorities (Rocks) with a named owner, KPIs, action plans, accountability. The practice is CEO-level (hired by the CEO, working with the leadership team), horizontal (no industry expertise required), and runs a 90-day refresh cadence anchored by a two-day annual session, continuing year after year. OneAccord pays for the Ninety licence while we are the client's active coach. Do not quote prices; price and scope go to the Managing Principal.

blocks.label: Try the diagnosis on a real company
blocks.instructions:
Pick one company you already know something about — a prospect, a client, or your own team.
  1. Write the three objectives as questions an owner would actually ask, in their words.
  2. Mark which one has pain, and note the sentence that told you so.
  3. Name the failure pattern you'd expect: no direction, misalignment, poor follow-through, or too busy and too close.
  4. Write the one question you'd ask next to confirm it.

Do this before your next conversation with them. You'll notice the difference in the first two minutes.
